crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Lecture materials from notes covers the practice of turning a lecturer's own written notes, slides and reading lists into a coherent set of teaching materials for a course. It sits inside course design and teaching, where the aim is a sequence of sessions, handouts and exercises that a student can follow without the lecturer present. The scope runs from a rough outline of topics through to the final set of slides, worked examples and assessment prompts. It also covers the reuse of last year's notes when a syllabus changes.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on ordinary document tools, a slide editor, a reference manager and the institution's learning management system. Notes are usually kept in a plain text or word processor file, with citations held in a manager such as Zotero or a BibTeX file, and figures stored separately so they can be redrawn. Where a course draws on published research, the source paper is the unit that gets cited, and a link should point at the original paper rather than at a search tool. Version control, even a simple dated folder, matters because notes change between terms.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The lecturer starts from the learning outcomes, then groups the notes into sessions and gives each session one idea, one worked example and one exercise. Drafting moves from outline to full prose to slides, with the prose kept as the master copy so the slides stay thin. Citations are attached at the point where a claim is made, and any figure taken from a paper is either redrawn or credited. A colleague or teaching assistant reads the draft for gaps before the term starts, and student questions during the term feed back into the notes.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights are the main constraint, because slides often reuse figures, tables and text from published work. Quoting a short passage with a clear citation is normal practice in teaching, while reproducing a full figure or a long extract usually needs permission or a redrawn version. Student work, recordings and any personal data in examples fall under the institution's privacy rules and must not be circulated outside the course. Provenance should be visible on every borrowed item, so a reader can trace a claim back to the paper it came from.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward notes that are structured enough to be reused across formats, so the same source produces slides, a handout and a question bank. Assistants that draft explanations or generate practice questions are being tried, which puts more weight on checking every generated claim against a real source. Departments are also asking for materials that can be shared between institutions, which pushes toward open licences and away from slides that quietly embed someone else's figure. The steady part is the citation habit, since a course built on traceable sources survives changes in tooling.
